claims.text: Robarge: Angleton 'ardently supported Israel'; his 'control of that country's account at CIA, an administrative anomaly, was one of the foundations of his influence'; 'he saw Israel as a bastion against the Soviet Union'; in 1954 he became head of the new Counterintelligence Staff.

Melman and Raviv: in 1951 Ben-Gurion met DCI Walter Bedell Smith and 'convinced U.S. intelligence to give Israel a try'; Angleton 'was put in charge of the U.S. side', with Amos Manor and Teddy Kollek as counterparts; the 1956 Khrushchev speech, obtained through an Israeli channel in Warsaw, was 'the great turning point'; Soviet-bloc immigrants made Israel 'an indispensable source'; Lakam ran Pollard; US law enforcement 'busted several conspiracies run by Israelis to procure defense and high-tech secrets'; Tenet tasked in 1996 with building Arafat's security forces.

Siskind: Grayevski borrowed the speech in Warsaw, Shin Bet agent Yaakov Barmor photographed it; Ben-Gurion sent it by courier to Israel's liaison Izzy Dorot; only Angleton was to see it; Dulles had it by mid-April 1956; CIA gave it to the NYT in early June 1956. Israel later lent the US a defected Iraqi MiG-21 (Have Donut), handed over a Soviet P-12 radar (1969) and a captured SA-6 battery (1973), and supplied detailed information on Soviet strategic missile forces in the early 1970s.

McConnell (1986): Angleton 'had exercised formal authority over CIA liaison with Israel' from the early 1950s (start disputed); the Israel desk sat under his CI staff, not the Near East division; a 1978 Senate Intelligence Committee study found the FBI investigated 'friendly' services only on specific complaints, information rarely reached prosecutors, and CIA and State discouraged penalties; John Davitt (DOJ, resigned 1980) told the NYT Israeli intelligence was 'the second most active' in the US after the Soviets.

FRUS: on 1 June 1967 Mossad chief Meir Amit met Defense Secretary McNamara (DDCI Rufus Taylor took notes); Amit called the Tiran blockade 'window dressing', said 'time is very much against Israel', estimated about 4,000 casualties, said his remarks were 'entirely informal, off the record'; McNamara said he would convey his views to the President.

entries.topic: The CIA's own concerns: NUMEC, the 1979 report, Pollard

claims.text: A 47-page CIA report on Israeli intelligence, reportedly seized at the US embassy in Tehran in 1979 and distributed by Iranian militants, was summarized by the Washington Post (Scott Armstrong) in Feb 1982; it said collection of secret US policy information ranked 'only second and third in priority' after the Arab states, and that collection was 'especially concentrated in the Soviet Union and the United States as well as the United Nations'. Begin's spokesman Uri Porat called it a 'cheap invention not worthy of comment'; a Jerusalem official said Iran 'cannot be described as a reliable source'.

CSM (2 Feb 1982): the Post and Boston Globe reported papers seized in Tehran saying Israeli agencies 'used blackmail, bugs, wiretaps, and bribe offers to US government employees'; the CIA had no comment.

CSM (6 Jun 1986): a former chief of DOJ's internal-security section said Israeli intelligence was the second most active foreign service in the US after the Soviets; a classified 1979 CIA report reportedly named secret US policy information and scientific intelligence as top priorities; Stansfield Turner: 'Of course it goes on'; Israel said the Pollard operation was unauthorized.

NUMEC: editors find 'strong but not incontrovertible evidence that a diversion did occur'; AEC (14 Feb 1966) 'found no evidence of theft'; 'The CIA has released none of its internal operational documents'; Helms asked AG Ramsey Clark on 2 Apr 1968 for a 'discreet intelligence investigation'; Hoover approved 6 May 1968 and told Helms on 3 Sep 1969 the FBI was discontinuing active investigation; Carl Duckett briefed the NRC in 1976 on the CIA's conclusion that Israel's first weapons 'owed in some measure to uranium from the NUMEC plant'; a March 1972 CIA memo called diversion 'a distinct possibility'; Brzezinski 1977: 'no evidence—despite an intensive search for some—to prove that one did'; GAO Dec 1978: 'a diversion could not be ruled out'; no official finding, no prosecution.

Pollard: CIA damage assessment of 30 Oct 1987; about 800 documents plus ~1,500 messages; taskings on Arab states, Pakistan and the USSR; Israelis 'never expressed interest in US military activities, plans, capabilities, or equipment'; LAKAM under Rafi Eitan; ISCAP ordered release in 2012; paroled 2015, released from parole November 2020. Tenet threatened to resign if Pollard were released (reported).

entries.topic: Iran, the peace process and the hostage channel; what the CIA cannot see

claims.text: Sanger (NYT 1 Jun 2012): Stuxnet was code-named Olympic Games, begun under Bush (2006); Unit 8200 provided technical expertise and intelligence on Natanz; the worm escaped via a programming error and was discovered in July 2010; Obama, briefed with Biden and CIA Director Panetta, chose to continue; the last attack took out nearly 1,000 of 5,000 centrifuges.

Sanger (NPR 4 Jun 2012): a beacon mapped Natanz and 'phoned home, back to the National Security Agency and the Unit 8200'; Bush 'didn't want to see the Israelis bomb the Iran facilities' and 'the Israelis needed to be convinced that there was an alternative to a military attack'; official estimate: 18 months to two years' delay.

Wye River Memorandum signed 23 Oct 1998; CRS: it creates 'an unusually visible role for the CIA'; Tenet was among the negotiators; trilateral committee meets at least biweekly; some Members of Congress concerned, SSCI planned hearings.

Burns met Barnea and Qatar PM in Doha on 9 Nov 2023 and 28 Nov 2023 (Egypt's Kamel also present); Burns's staff in contact with a joint Israeli-Qatari 'situation room' at Mossad HQ; original deal 50 hostages for four-day pause. Paris talks 28 Jan 2024 with Burns, Barnea, Al-Thani, Kamel and Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar on a two-month pause framework.

Roman Gofman, with 'no prior intelligence background', became Mossad director on 2 June 2026, replacing David Barnea at the end of his five-year term; about two weeks before 22 Jul 2026 he met CIA Director John Ratcliffe and White House officials in Washington on Iran; CIA and Mossad declined comment.

WSJ (8 Apr 2024): a secret White House memorandum after Oct 7 expanded sharing, including raw intelligence such as live drone feeds over Gaza; the US expanded its own collection on Gaza, having previously relied largely on Israel; US does not share intelligence intended specifically for ground or air strikes; Israel certifies its own compliance, sometimes orally; officials say it is hard to know how US intelligence is used once combined with Israel's data; Hagari: 'unprecedented levels of intelligence coordination'.

Reuters (Dec 2025): in the second half of 2024 the US cut a live drone feed over Gaza for at least a few days and restricted how Israel could use some intelligence on high-value targets, over civilian deaths and Shin Bet treatment of prisoners; sharing resumed after assurances; Biden declined a more formal cutoff; IDF: 'The strategic intelligence cooperation continued throughout the war.'

Reuters (Nov 2025): US intelligence gathered in 2024 indicated Israeli military lawyers warned of evidence that could support war-crimes charges; an NSC meeting in Dec 2024; lawyers concluded it remained legal to keep supplying weapons and intelligence because the US had not gathered its own evidence of violations; Israel denies war crimes; State: 'We do not comment on intelligence matters.'
